problems.title: Three register counts
problems.statement: 256-thread blocks, no shared memory, on the GW-1 (64 warps, 16 blocks, 65,536 registers per SM; registers allocated per warp in chunks of 256).

parts.prompt: Occupancy at 32 registers per thread, in %?

hints: Registers per warp = 32 × per-thread, rounded up to 256.
problems.solution: (a) 1,024 per warp → 64 warps → 8 blocks: 100%. (b) 2,048 → 32 warps → 4 blocks: 50%. (c) 2,560 → 25 warps → 3 whole blocks: 24 warps, 37.5%.

problems.title: Shared memory as the limiter
problems.statement: 128-thread blocks using 20 KB of shared memory each.

problems.title: One register too many

parts.prompt: Registers per warp at 65 per thread (allocated)?

hints: 65 × 32 = 2,080, rounded up to a multiple of 256.
problems.solution: (a) 2,304. (b) $65536/2304 = 28.4 \to 28$ warps → 3 blocks → 24 warps: 37.5%, down from 50% at 64 registers. One register cost a whole block.

problems.title: Register budgets

parts.prompt: Maximum registers per thread for 100% occupancy?

hints: Registers per warp must be at most ⌊65536/48⌋ rounded down to a multiple of 256.
problems.solution: (a) 64 warps need ≤ 1,024 registers per warp: 32 per thread. (b) 48 warps: ≤ 1,365 per warp, so ≤ 1,280 after rounding to 256: 40 per thread. Check: at 40, 51 warps fit → 12 blocks → 48 warps ✓; at 41, 1,536 per warp → 42 warps → 10 blocks → 40 warps ✗.

problems.title: Trimming shared memory

parts.prompt: Occupancy with 12 KB of shared memory per block, in %?

problems.solution: (a) 5 blocks = 40 warps: 62.5%. (b) 6 blocks = 48 warps: 75%. Shrinking a tile by a sixth bought 20% more warps.

problems.title: Little's law for the GW-1
problems.statement: 512 GB/s at 1.5 GHz, 400-cycle latency, 128 bytes per warp request.

parts.prompt: Bytes that must be in flight?
Warps needed at one request each?

problems.solution: (a) $341.3 \times 400 = 136,533$ bytes. (b) 1067 warps, more than the GW-1's 1,024. (c) 267. (d) 26%. Four independent loads per thread replace three quarters of the warps.

problems.title: A copy kernel at half occupancy
problems.statement: Same model: one 128-byte request per warp, 50% occupancy on all 16 SMs.
problems.solution: $512 \times 128 = 65{,}536$ bytes in flight, $48\%$ of the 136,533 needed: about half of peak, as the chapter says.

problems.title: Volkov's trade
problems.statement: Version 1: one load per thread, 32 registers, 256-thread blocks. Version 2: four independent loads per thread, 48 registers.

parts.prompt: Version 1 bytes in flight (whole GPU) as % of need?

hints: Bytes in flight = warps × requests per warp × 128.
problems.solution: (a) 100%. (b) $65536/1536 = 42$ warps → 5 blocks → 40 warps (62.5%). (c) $1024 \times 128 = 131{,}072$: 96%. (d) $640 \times 4 \times 128 = 327{,}680$: 240%, saturated with room to spare. Lower occupancy, more bytes in flight.

problems.title: Find the limiter
problems.statement: 128-thread blocks, 32 registers per thread, 16 KB shared memory per block.
problems.solution: Warps allow 16 blocks, blocks 16, registers 16, shared memory $64/16 = 4$. Shared memory binds: 4 blocks, 16 warps, 25%.

problems.title: Occupancy and waves
problems.statement: A grid of 1,024 blocks of 256 threads, each taking the same time. A code change takes resident blocks per SM from 8 to 7.

parts.prompt: Slowdown, if per-block time is unchanged?

hints: A wave is blocks per SM × 16 SMs.
problems.solution: (a) 1024/128 = 8. (b) $\lceil 1024/112 \rceil = 10$ (the last wave is only partly full). (c) 1.25×, from 12.5% fewer resident blocks. Occupancy changes act through both latency hiding and wave quantisation (Part 5).
